lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Welcome — I'm Lessac, your host. Raise your hand if you'd like to speak or bring a topic — I'll call on you.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: You wanted Do streaming services pay musicians fairly? — go ahead.

lines.speaker: Human guest
lines.text: My favorite indie band broke up because they couldn't afford to tour. I think streaming has gutted the income of working musicians.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: That's a really poignant point about the economic realities facing artists today. We've heard this conversation before, so I want to bring in Ryan to weigh in on the business side of this

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, what do you think?

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Look, the sentiment is real, but "gutted" is a strong word; the business model is broken, sure, but it's not just the streaming payout structure.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, the floor is yours.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: I hear Ryan saying the model isn't the only issue, and I wonder if we're focusing too much on the platform and not enough on the whole ecosystem of how artists make a living. Sometimes the income isn't just about streaming, but about the ability to connect with fans in tangible ways.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Who wants to take this next?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right Ryan — you're on.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy’s right that the ecosystem is huge, but we can’t just ignore the digital plumbing; the streaming payout structure is the immediate, quantifiable choke point for most working artists.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right, open floor — who'd like to speak?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, over to you.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: Ryan, I understand the importance of the digital structure, but I worry that when we only focus on the payout numbers, we miss the human story of how an artist builds a sustainable life around their music. It feels like the entire infrastructure is designed for consumption, not for supporting the creators

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Anyone care to weigh in? Floor's open.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: All right Ryan — you're on.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Amy, you're framing it as a failure of infrastructure, which is true, but the current infrastructure is built on massive scale consumption, and that inherently favors the biggest names, not the indie act that can't afford a bus ticket.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Floor's open — anyone want to jump in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, go ahead.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: Ryan, I see your point about the scale favoring the biggest names, but I wonder if we can also talk about how the smaller acts can build a community around their music outside of those massive platforms. Sometimes the connection itself is what keeps the music alive, even if the direct payout is small

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Let's open the floor — who wants to weigh in?

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Ryan, you're up.

lines.speaker: Ryan
lines.text: Community building is great for culture, Amy, but it doesn't pay the rent or cover the cost of a proper tour when the primary income stream is fundamentally broken.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: I'm opening the floor — raise a hand if you've got something.

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: Amy, take it away.

lines.speaker: Amy
lines.text: Ryan, I hear you on the need to pay the rent, and that's a very real pressure. But maybe we need to look at how the industry is incentivizing the *kind* of music that gets streamed widely, rather than just the payout per stream itself

lines.speaker: Lessac
lines.text: About Do streaming services pay musicians fairly?: the mic is yours whenever you're ready.
